title: Getting started

body:
The rebuild entry point is a Dagger module in this repository. Everything it runs, it runs in containers it puts together, so the machine that calls it needs only two tools, and the module needs to know where the values checkout is.
The Dagger CLI The CLI has to be the version the module pins. That’s v1.0.0-beta.15, the engineVersion in the repository’s dagger-module.toml. Install it with Dagger’s install script, at that version:
curl -fsSL https://dl.dagger.io/dagger/install.sh \ | DAGGER_VERSION=1.0.0-beta.15 BIN_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin" sh Check that the CLI on your PATH is the right one:
dagger version It should report v1.0.0-beta.15. Dagger 1.0 is in beta, and the module moves to a newer engine only when a pull request moves it. Install a newer CLI then, too.
A container runtime The CLI runs the Dagger engine as a container, and the engine runs every step of a run in containers of its own. Any runtime the Dagger CLI can start the engine with works, such as Docker or Podman. The CLI starts the engine on the first call and reuses it after that.
The values checkout The values checkout is a git repository of its own, outside this one. It holds a file per target, targets/<name>.yaml, which says whether the target is live or a drill:
targets/ live.yaml kind: live drill.yaml kind: drill A Dagger function can’t read the machine it’s called from, so the module takes the checkout as an argument. Set it once, from this repository’s checkout, as a user-level Dagger setting:
dagger settings -g rebuild values ../infra-values -g keeps the setting out of the repository: Dagger writes it to ~/.config/dagger/config.toml, keyed by this repository’s git remote, so nothing about your machine is committed. Every dagger call in a checkout of this repository then uses it. Check it with:
dagger settings rebuild To work on the module Go is needed only to change the module’s code, not to run it. The module’s go.mod files name the Go version.
Next: A first drill

title: What you need

body:
A drill is a rebuild against a scratch target, which leaves the live platform untouched. Drill and live differ only in the target, so a drill is the same commands a live rebuild runs. Run them from this repository’s checkout, with the values checkout set as What you need says.
Add the drill’s target Give the drill a file in the values checkout, targets/drill.yaml:
kind: drill The name of the file, without .yaml, is the target’s name. A drill may run from uncommitted changes, in either checkout, so the file doesn’t need to be committed first. The run’s record says it was.
Check the target dagger call preflight --target drill It changes nothing. Against a target that holds nothing yet, it prints:
the preflight check passed against drill. It fails if the target’s last run didn’t finish, or if a phase that run applied no longer verifies. The preflight check says what each means.
Run it dagger call up --target drill up runs the preflight check, then applies and verifies the first phase, and stops at the checkpoint after it. dagger call prints the run’s summary: each phase the call ran, what it made and how long it took, the run’s time so far, and what you can do next. At the checkpoint after phase 0, it reads like this:
run 7QH3W2Y5N4RJXK6VZ2B4TQ3MJE against drill phase 0: verified, 2m31.4s made the state backend, bucket drill-state the run's time so far: 2m40.2s the run paused at the checkpoint after phase 0. Continue with up --resume, or tear the target down with down. Look at what the phase made. Then continue with the next phase:
dagger call up --target drill --resume Each call runs one phase and stops at the checkpoint after it, until the last phase verifies and the summary says so:
the run finished: every phase verified. No phase has landed yet, so today the first up finishes at once, with nothing to do:
run JCUPWNYUR4NCJ3NCOSRCBM5DKF against drill the run took 829.009578ms the run finished: every phase verified. Two flags change where a call stops:
--no-pause runs on from one phase to the next without stopping, so each phase’s verify is the only gate. --through <phase> stops after the phase it names, such as --through 0. The run is then unfinished, and --resume continues it. After a failure A failed apply or verify stops the run at once. up fails with what failed, followed by the summary, and leaves the target as it is for you to look at:
the run failed at phase 1a's verify: <what failed> Once the target is fit to resume, continue with up --resume, which applies phase 1a again. Or tear the target down with down. From there, either:
resume, once the target is fit to: fix what failed, in either checkout if it needs a change, and run up --resume. It verifies every phase the run already verified, then applies the failed phase again and goes on. If an earlier phase no longer verifies, it stops, changing nothing. tear down, with down, below, and start again with a fresh up. up without --resume refuses to start a new run on top of an unfinished one.
Tear it down dagger call down --target drill down tears down every phase in reverse order, phase 0 last, and leaves the target as a rebuild from nothing. It succeeds when there’s nothing left, and it’s safe to run again after it fails partway.
Next: Going live

title: Fundamentals

body:
Keeping Dagger current The rebuild entry point is a Dagger module, and these pin the Dagger it runs on:
engineVersion, in every dagger-module.toml: the repository root’s, for the module, and rebuild/tests/dagger-module.toml, for its tests. It pins the engine. DAGGER_VERSION, in .github/workflows/build.yaml: the CLI that Build installs. What you need tells the operator to install the same version. dagger.lock: every image and git ref the workspace uses, by digest or commit. That includes the Go SDK that writes the module’s generated code, and devex’s modules, which the module’s checks run. Nothing moves any of them except a pull request.
Moving the engine Move engineVersion and the CLI pin in Build together, in one pull request, along with the version on What you need. .github/scripts/check-dagger-pin.sh fails Build when they differ. Then install the same CLI version locally, as that page says, and regenerate the module’s code:
dagger generate -y Commit whatever it changes. The Go SDK’s check, dagger-go-sdk:stale, fails Build when the committed code isn’t what dagger generate writes.
Moving the pins in dagger.lock dagger lock update resolves the entries again, moving tags and branches to what they point at now:
dagger lock update # every entry dagger lock update --list # the selectors it knows dagger lock update devex # just devex's modules It regenerates the module’s code as well. Run the checks, then commit dagger.lock with what changed:
dagger check dagger -m rebuild/tests check --module tests The engine adds an entry for anything it resolves that dagger.lock doesn’t record. Build fails when a run leaves dagger.lock changed, so a new image or module is committed with its pin.
Why this matters more while Dagger is in beta Dagger 1.0 is in beta, and a beta can change between releases: a module’s API, what the Go SDK generates, how a check runs. Pinned, none of that reaches a rebuild until a pull request brings it in, and Build runs the module’s checks on it first. Moving often, a release at a time, keeps each change small enough to see what broke. Left for months, the move becomes several breaking releases at once, and a rebuild is the worst time to find that the pinned version is no longer published.

title: Routine maintenance

body:
The platform is rebuilt, not repaired. One module in this repository stands it up from nothing, one phase at a time, against one named target, and tears it down again in reverse.
The command The rebuild is three functions of the rebuild Dagger module, which dagger.toml makes the workspace’s entry point. Run them from this repository’s checkout:
dagger call up --target <name> [--resume] [--through <phase>] [--no-pause] dagger call down --target <name> [--confirm <name>] dagger call preflight --target <name> up runs the preflight check, then applies and verifies phases in order. It stops at a checkpoint after each phase. --no-pause runs on without stopping, and --through names the last phase it runs. With --resume, it continues the target’s unfinished run instead of starting a new one. down tears down every phase in reverse order, phase 0 last. It’s safe to run again after it fails partway, and it succeeds when there’s nothing left. preflight runs only the preflight check, and changes nothing. There’s no default target: each function refuses to run without --target. None of them is ever served from Dagger’s cache, and neither is any command a phase runs against a target, so every call really reads and changes the target it names.
Targets A target is the one place a run is pointed at, such as the live platform or a scratch drill. Drill and live differ only in the target. Each has a file in the values checkout, targets/<name>.yaml, which says which it is:
kind: drill kind is live or drill. The file is read strictly: a key it shouldn’t have, a second YAML document or any other kind is refused, and so is a target with no file. The rest of the file, the values each phase reads, comes with phase 0.
Only one target is live. Every call reads every target’s file, as the values checkout’s commit has it and as the checkout stands, and refuses to run when more than one target is live. A target is live when either version of its file says so, so an uncommitted edit can’t turn the live target into a drill.
The values checkout is a git repository outside this one. A Dagger function can’t read the machine it’s called from, so the module takes the checkout as an argument, which the operator sets once as a user-level Dagger setting; see What you need.
Three rules keep a drill off the live platform:
There’s no default target. A run against the live target refuses uncommitted changes, in this repository or in the values checkout, so every change to the live platform was made from history. A drill may run from uncommitted changes, and its record says so. down against the live target needs --confirm <name>. A drill doesn’t, but refuses a name that isn’t its own. The phase order Each phase is one part of the platform. The order is fixed in one place, rebuild/phases.go:
Phase Part 0 the state backend 1a the cloud anchor and the edge 1b the operations tunnel 1c home-lab hosts 2 tenant compute, then the offerings tenants use 3 backup, and observability 4 the canary tenant A phase joins the order when its part lands, and a rebuild runs every phase the order holds. No phase has landed yet, so the order is empty: up against any target passes the preflight check as a rebuild from nothing, and finishes with nothing to do.
The phase contract Every phase meets one interface, in rebuild/run/:
Apply makes the target match the phase’s definitions. Verify fails unless the target is what the phase last applied, and it works. Teardown removes everything Apply made. It succeeds when there’s nothing left to remove, including when Apply never ran. Each runs against one target, and each is safe to run again after it fails partway. A phase reads every value it needs from the target, and nothing from the machine the run started on.
Checkpoints A Dagger function runs to completion, so a checkpoint is the end of a call, not a prompt inside one.
After each phase verifies, up writes the run’s record and returns a summary, which dagger call prints: what the phase made, how long it took, and the run’s time so far. Then it stops. The operator chooses:
continue, with up --resume, which runs the next phase; tear down, with down. With --no-pause, as in CI and in drills, up doesn’t stop between phases. Each phase’s verify is then the only gate.
A failed apply or verify stops the run at once. up writes the record and fails with what failed, followed by the summary, and leaves the target as it is to look at.
Resuming A run that stopped, at a checkpoint, where --through said, or on a failure, is unfinished. up --resume:
stops unless the target’s last run is unfinished; runs Verify for every phase the run has verified so far, and stops on any failure, because that’s drift; continues from the first phase that didn’t verify, starting with its Apply. Whether a target is fit to resume is the operator’s call. A failure can leave a phase in a state its Apply can’t fix. Resuming then fails again, and down followed by a fresh up is the way back.
A resumed run is the same run, with the same ID. It may resume from a different commit than it started from, such as one that fixes the phase that failed, and its record keeps the commits each phase was applied from.
The preflight check Before up applies anything, it checks the target. preflight runs the same check on its own.
If the target has no state backend, this is a rebuild from nothing, and the check passes. If the target’s last run is unfinished, the check stops. up never starts a new run on top of one: resume it with up --resume, or tear the target down with down. Otherwise it runs Verify for every phase the last run applied. Any failure is drift, and the check stops before anything changes. Drift is a difference between the target and what the rebuild last applied to it. A difference between what was last applied and today’s definitions isn’t drift: it’s the change this run applies.
Records Each run keeps a record in the target’s state backend, which phase 0 makes. It holds:
the commits of this repository and of the values checkout that each phase was applied from, and whether either had uncommitted changes; each phase it applied, what the phase made and how long it took; where it stopped, at a checkpoint, where --through said or on a failure, or that it finished. The record of the last run that finished is the target’s last-known-good. The record lives only in the target, and down removes it with phase 0. Until phase 0 lands, no target has a state backend, so no run is recorded and every up is a rebuild from nothing.
Time A rebuild is meant to take at most 60 minutes. A run’s time is measured from the start of its first up to the last phase’s verify. It includes the preflight check, the time between calls at every checkpoint, and the time between a failure and its resume. The summary shows each phase’s time and the run’s, and marks a run over 60 minutes, and the record keeps both.
A run is never stopped for time. A live rebuild that’s running long is still the fastest way back.
Next: The platform

body:
Going live is the same rebuild a drill runs, against the live target. The commands are the same; what changes is the target, and two rules that keep a drill from ever reaching it by mistake.
Add the live target Give the live target a file in the values checkout, targets/live.yaml:
kind: live Only one target is live: every call refuses to run while a second target’s file says kind: live, as committed or as it stands.
Commit everything first A run against the live target refuses uncommitted changes, in this repository or in the values checkout, so every change to the live platform is made from history. Commit both, and check that neither has anything left over:
git status git -C ../infra-values status Otherwise up stops before it changes anything:
a run against the live target refuses uncommitted changes: the target's values have uncommitted changes Check the target dagger call preflight --target live It changes nothing, and prints that the check passed. If the target’s last run didn’t finish, or a phase that run applied no longer verifies, it fails and says which. See The preflight check.
Run it dagger call up --target live As in a drill, up applies and verifies one phase, stops at the checkpoint after it, and prints the run’s summary: what the phase made, how long it took and the run’s time so far. Look at what the phase made, then continue:
dagger call up --target live --resume Each call runs the next phase, until the summary says the run finished and every phase verified. That run is the target’s last-known-good. A live rebuild is meant to take at most 60 minutes, counting the time spent at checkpoints. The summary marks a run that went over, and it’s never stopped for time.
After a failure A failed apply or verify stops the run at once, prints what failed with the summary, and leaves the target as it is. Look at what failed, then either:
resume, once the target is fit to: commit the fix, in whichever checkout needs it, and run up --resume. It verifies every phase the run already verified, then applies the failed phase again and goes on. tear down, and start again with a fresh up. Tearing it down down against the live target needs the target’s name, to confirm it:
dagger call down --target live --confirm live Without --confirm live it refuses:
down was not confirmed with the target's name: live is the live target; confirm with "live" to tear it down It refuses uncommitted changes too, as up does. It tears down every phase in reverse order, phase 0 last, and it’s safe to run again after it fails partway.
Next: Fundamentals

body:
infra defines a self-hosted application platform: the place the operator’s own capabilities run by default, so that none of them depends on a vendor’s hosting product.
It’s rebuilt, not repaired. The platform can be stood up from nothing, from this repository, in at most 60 minutes. It’s self-hosted, not self-owned. It spans a public cloud and the home lab. “Self-hosted” means the operator controls it end to end, not that every part runs on hardware the operator owns. It’s run by one operator, in at most 2 hours a week. A designated successor holds sealed credentials and uses them only if the operator can’t. Its tenants are the operator’s capabilities. Their end users reach the tenants, never the platform. The platform is being rebuilt from scratch, as the charter sets out.
Reading order The site reads in the order its readers need it: the operator first, then a successor who has to take over, then a capability owner bringing a tenant.
Getting started: standing the platform up from nothing, first as a drill and then live. Fundamentals: the ideas every part of the platform builds on. The platform: one page per part, in the order a rebuild stands them up. Operating: running the platform day to day, handing it to a successor, and recovering it. Hosting a tenant: what a capability owner needs to run a tenant on the platform. Start with Getting started.
